claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure containing a ductile soft phase and a reinforcing hard phase.
An annealing treatment just above the soft phase's recrystallization onset can selectively recrystallize the soft phase while leaving the hard phase intact.
The treatment produces a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded within a hard-phase skeleton.
The hard-phase skeleton remains unaltered by the treatment.
Selective annealing relieves accumulated dislocations at phase boundaries.
Relieving boundary dislocations reduces dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations.
Reduced boundary stress concentrations prevent microcracking during subsequent deformation.
The retained hard-phase network continues to impart high strength.
Phase-selective recrystallization markedly improves tensile ductility relative to the untreated eutectic alloy.
The treated alloy may approach approximately 35% uniform elongation.
The treated alloy may achieve true stress near or above 2 GPa.
The treatment retains or increases strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Untreated eutectic alloys exhibit limited ductility.
The untreated alloy's limited room-temperature ductility is caused by dislocation pile-ups at dual-phase interfaces, local stress concentrations, and premature microcracking.
The untreated alloy maintains high strength despite its limited ductility.
The predicted improvement applies to room-temperature tensile testing under quasi-static loading.
Excessive annealing may cause unwanted grain growth or adversely affect the hard phase.
Insufficient annealing may fail to relieve boundary dislocations effectively.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis allows strength to be retained rather than increased, but the falsification rule treats no improvement in tensile strength as falsifying. Unchanged strength combined with improved ductility would satisfy the stated prediction yet fail the stated test.
